source.versionTitle: Atra-ḫasīs, Tablet II — best-effort reconstruction from named scholarly editions
source.verificationStatus: best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification. Reconstructed from the standard scholarly editions (Lambert & Millard 1969, the critical edition; George & Al-Rawi 1996 for the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.). Line numbering follows Lambert–Millard 1969, which number Tablet II by COLUMN + line (II i 1, II ii 1 …) rather than the continuous scheme used for Tablet I; refIds accordingly take the form ATRA-WOH-II:<column>-<line> (see the chapter editorial_questions). The eBL corpus L.1.1 (ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1) and SEAL served as a collation aid only (CC BY-NC — not reproduced). Tablet II is the MOST DAMAGED of the three tablets: the sign-by-sign transliteration is a best-effort reconstruction and is PENDING COLLATION against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1; per-line sign values may contain reconstruction errors, and confidence here is LOWER than for Tablet I. The narrative SPINE — the population-growth refrain, the clamor (rigmu/ḫubūru) that robs Enlil of sleep, the successive afflictions (plague via Namtar; drought via Adad withholding rain; famine), Enki's offering-concentration stratagem, and the escalation to the flood and the oath — is well-attested across the cited editions and should match the downstream English faithfully. Columns v (the years-of-famine catalogue) and vi–viii (the assembly, the accusation of Ea, the flood-decree, and the oath) are heavily broken and are given in OUTLINE ONLY, honestly marked with lacuna objects.

source.fragmentationNote: Atra-ḫasīs is a three-tablet Old Babylonian epic (c. 1700 BCE), best preserved in the copy of the scribe Ku-Aya / Ipiq-Aya (reign of Ammi-ṣaduqa). Tablet II carries the central population-control cycle: the land grows wide and the people multiply until their clamor (rigmu / ḫubūru) disturbs Enlil and robs him of sleep, whereupon he sends successive afflictions to thin humankind — first plague/pestilence (through Namtar), then drought (ordering Adad to withhold the rain and the springs, so the black fields whiten and the plain brings forth salt), then famine — each over the recurring interval (~1200 years). Each time the sage Atra-ḫasīs appeals to his god Enki/Ea, who counsels the people to withhold reverence from all the gods and concentrate every offering on the single deity responsible, so that god, shamed by the gift, lifts the scourge. Enlil, repeatedly thwarted and enraged at Ea's circumvention, escalates to the final solution — the abūbu (flood) — and binds the gods by oath to secrecy; the flood proper belongs to Tablet III. Tablet II is the MOST DAMAGED of the three: this file reconstructs the attested spine and marks the badly-broken stretches (col v famine-catalogue; cols vi–viii assembly, accusation, flood-decree, oath) with honest lacuna objects and outline-only renderings. This is a MOAT TEXT: no usable public-domain English translation of Atra-ḫasīs exists, so the Wheel of Heaven program renders its own English from the Akkadian.

segments.label: Column i — the land grows wide; the clamor of humankind robs Enlil of sleep (Lambert–Millard II i 1–8)

notes: *mātu rapāšu* 'the land grew broad'; *nišū mâdu* 'the people became many.' The opening of Tablet II states the population-growth premise plainly.
*šapû* 'to be(come) loud, to bellow'; *lû* 'bull.' The din-of-humankind simile.
*ḫubūru* 'clamor, uproar, din' (no glossary entry — see editorial questions); *adāru* (N) 'to be disturbed, troubled.'
*rigmu* 'noise, cry, clamor' (no glossary entry — see editorial questions); *šemû* 'to hear.'
Speech-introduction; *ilū rabûtum* 'the great gods.'
*kabātu* 'to be(come) heavy, burdensome'; *rigim awīlūti* 'the noise of humankind.' The population-as-problem thesis stated in Enlil's own mouth.
*zamû* 'to be deprived of'; *šittu* 'sleep.' The divine-repose-disturbed motif (cf. Gilgamesh XI); on *ḫubūru* see editorial questions.
*šuruppû* 'chills, frost-disease' (an affliction-term; no glossary entry — see editorial questions). The first population-reduction is a pestilence.

preceding_lacuna.text: The final movement of Tablet II (the escalation from the failed lesser afflictions to the flood, and the oath) survives only in part and continues into Tablet III. The spine — the decree of the abūbu (flood) as the final population-solution, and the oath of secrecy binding the gods — is given in outline.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection / damage: the flood-decree and oath survive in part and continue into Tablet III; given here in outline.]

notes: Speech-introduction.
Speech-introduction.

*abūbu* 'the Flood' (central flood-vocabulary; the final solution); *napḫaru* 'totality'; *nišū* 'people.' The population-control escalates from plague and famine to annihilation — the cause is the noise, not moral corruption (contrast Genesis; see editorial questions).
*māmītu* 'oath, curse-bound oath'; *leqû* 'to take.' Enlil demands the gods swear to secrecy.
*tamû* (D) 'to make swear, bind by oath'; the oath of secrecy imposed on the whole pantheon.
Enki is bound by the same oath — the tension that in Tablet III he resolves by speaking the plan not to Atra-ḫasīs but to the reed-wall, keeping the letter of the oath while circumventing it.
